overview.title: 📖 Overview: What Counts as a Valid 'Lamb'
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 12a–12b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna lists animals unfit to redeem a firstborn donkey — a calf, an undomesticated animal, a slaughtered animal, a tereifa, a hybrid, and a koy — deriving the whole list from a verbal analogy to the Paschal lamb. The Gemara then tests the boundary with four unresolved edge cases, before addressing a structural safeguard: a priest may not simply take an unredeemed donkey on his own promise to redeem it later. A second mishna raises what happens if the designated lamb dies before reaching the priest, and the daf closes by fixing exactly when redemption must take place.

slides.title: 🚫 Which Animals May Not Redeem a Firstborn Donkey?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's list, and Rabbi Eliezer's exceptions
rows: A calf or an undomesticated animal (חַיָּה)
A slaughtered animal or a tereifa

callout.label: Source (ben Bag Bag):
callout.text: The word 'seh' (lamb) used here for redemption is linked, by verbal analogy, to the same word used for the Paschal offering (Exodus 12:3) — whatever is excluded there is excluded here.

slides.title: 🤔 Four Borderline Cases: Good Enough to Redeem With?
slides.subtitle: Testing the edges of the mishna's categories

nodes.content: ❓ A ben pekua — a lamb removed alive from its ritually slaughtered mother's womb. A slaughtered animal, or a true living lamb?

columns.label: Mar Zutra
columns.content: Forbidden — legally like 'meat in a basket,' as if already slaughtered

columns.label: Rav Ashi
columns.content: Permitted — it currently runs and lives, so it is called 'a lamb'

nodes.content: 🐐 A 'nidmeh' — born of two sheep parents but looking like a goat. Does the ban on a true hybrid extend to this merely goat-looking lamb too? Left open
⛔ Disqualified consecrated animals: Rav Mari links their verse ('like the gazelle and the hart') to the same phrase excluding wild game from redemption
🌾 An animal bought with Sabbatical-year produce: certainly forbidden for a definite firstborn; genuinely uncertain for an uncertain one

slides.title: 🤝 Why Must the Priest Redeem in the Owner's Presence?
slides.subtitle: A baraita's safeguard, and what it reveals

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: If a priest tells an Israelite, 'give me your firstborn donkey and I'll redeem it myself' — the Israelite may not hand it over unless the priest redeems it right there, in front of him.

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman
lines.text: This teaches something real: priests in general are suspected of using a firstborn donkey for labor without ever redeeming it!

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Isn't that obvious from the baraita's own words?

lines.speaker: Clarified
lines.text: You might think this suspicion applies only to a known offender. Rav Naḥman teaches it applies to every priest — the lamb stays his either way, whether or not he ever redeems the donkey.

slides.title: 💀 If the Designated Lamb Dies First
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis, and Abaye's sharp challenge

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Eliezer: the owner bears responsibility and must supply another lamb — like the five sela for a firstborn son, still owed even if the money is lost
2️⃣ The Rabbis: no responsibility — like money set aside for second-tithe produce, desanctified the instant it's designated

3️⃣ Abaye challenges Rabbi Eliezer: if compared to a firstborn son, benefit from an unredeemed donkey should be permitted too — yet you rule it must be buried if it dies, implying benefit is forbidden!
4️⃣ Rava resolves: the comparison to a firstborn son applies only to financial responsibility for the lamb — not to whether one may derive benefit from the donkey. Two separate questions

slides.title: ⏰ When Must a Firstborn Donkey Be Redeemed?
slides.subtitle: Reconciling two seemingly contradictory baraitot
rows: Means: if redeemed right away, it is valid — not that one must redeem instantly
Another baraita: no redemption before 30 days, though one may extend indefinitely after
Sets the ideal, latest-not-earliest timing — paralleling a firstborn son's redemption

callout.label: Rav Naḥman's reconciliation:
callout.text: Redeeming immediately is effective after the fact, even though the ideal practice is to wait thirty days — just as redeeming a firstborn son within his first thirty days is likewise effective, though not the ideal timing.

summary.principle: Only a genuine lamb, derived by verbal analogy from the Paschal offering, may redeem a firstborn donkey; the redemption must ultimately be completed, with the owner and the priest each bearing distinct responsibilities and both able to act immediately, though the ideal timing is after thirty days.

flowSteps.content: 🚫 The mishna excludes calves, wild animals, slaughtered animals, tereifot, hybrids, and koys from redeeming a firstborn donkey
🤔 Edge cases tested: a ben pekua, a goat-looking lamb, disqualified sacrifices, and Sabbatical-year animals

columns.content: 🤝 A priest must redeem the donkey in the owner's presence — priests are suspected otherwise
💀 R' Eliezer and the Rabbis dispute who bears the loss if the lamb dies before reaching the priest

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: redemption may happen immediately and remain valid, though the ideal practice waits until the donkey is thirty days old

quiz.q: According to ben Bag Bag, from where is the mishna's list of animals unfit to redeem a firstborn donkey derived?
o: From a direct verse listing each animal by name
From a verbal analogy between the word 'lamb' used for redemption and the same word used for the Paschal offering
From an oral tradition with no textual source
From the laws of animal tithes
quiz.e: Ben Bag Bag derives the exclusion list via a verbal analogy: since 'lamb' (seh) in the Paschal offering excludes these categories of animals, the same word used for redeeming a firstborn donkey excludes them too.

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi regarding redeeming a firstborn donkey with a ben pekua (a lamb removed alive from its slaughtered mother)?
o: Both permit it without dispute
Mar Zutra forbids it, treating it as already-slaughtered meat; Rav Ashi permits it since it currently lives and runs
Both forbid it entirely
The dispute concerns only its monetary value
quiz.e: Mar Zutra treats the ben pekua as equivalent to slaughtered meat and forbids using it for redemption, while Rav Ashi holds that since it is alive and moving, it qualifies as a genuine lamb.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman, what does the requirement that a priest redeem a firstborn donkey in the owner's presence actually teach?
o: That priests cannot be trusted with any monetary transactions
That priests in general are suspected of using a firstborn donkey without ever redeeming it, since the lamb remains theirs either way
That only some specific priests are untrustworthy
That the owner must always be a Levite
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman teaches this suspicion applies broadly to every priest, not just a known offender, since a priest benefits from keeping the donkey unredeemed just as much as from redeeming it.

quiz.q: How does Rava resolve Abaye's challenge that Rabbi Eliezer's comparison of a firstborn donkey to a firstborn son should also permit deriving benefit from an unredeemed donkey?
o: He concedes benefit is permitted after all
He explains the comparison applies only to financial responsibility for a lost lamb, not to the permissibility of deriving benefit from the donkey
He rejects Rabbi Eliezer's opinion entirely
He says a firstborn son also requires burial if he dies
quiz.e: Rava limits the son-donkey comparison strictly to the question of who bears financial loss for the redemption lamb, keeping it separate from the unrelated question of deriving benefit from the donkey itself.

quiz.q: How does Rav Naḥman reconcile the baraita stating redemption is 'immediate' with the one stating it doesn't apply before thirty days?
o: He says the two baraitot simply contradict each other with no resolution
'Immediate' means redeeming right away is valid after the fact, even though the ideal practice is to wait until thirty days
He rules that only the thirty-day baraita is authoritative
He says immediate redemption applies only to firstborn sons
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman explains that redeeming immediately is effective if done, but the preferred, ideal practice is to wait until the donkey is thirty days old — paralleling the redemption of a firstborn son.
